scenes.head: Capital structure
scenes.sub: Does borrowing make a business more valuable? Work through Modigliani and Miller’s answer without and with taxes, then the costs of financial distress, the trade-off and pecking-order theories, agency costs and covenants, and what finance directors say they actually do.

segs.say: Capital structure. Does borrowing make a business more valuable? Work through Modigliani and Miller’s answer without and with taxes, then the costs of financial distress, the trade-off and pecking-order theories, agency costs and covenants, and what finance directors say they actually do.

scenes.head: You will be able to

segs.say: Compare debt and equity as claims on a business: priority, control, taxes, covenants and flexibility.
Calculate how financial leverage changes earnings per share and return on equity, and find the EBIT at which two financing plans give the same EPS.
Apply Modigliani and Miller’s propositions without taxes, and explain the homemade-leverage argument behind them.
Calculate the present value of the interest tax shield, the levered firm’s value V_L = V_U + T D, and the cost of equity with corporate tax.
Explain the costs of financial distress, the trade-off and pecking-order theories, and the agency costs of debt and equity, and evaluate them against survey evidence.

scenes.head: Ana has financed Lantern in three ways so far: her own $20,000 of shares, profit kept in the business, and borrowing (Coastline Bank’s loans, the…

segs.say: Ana has financed Lantern in three ways so far: her own $20,000 of shares, profit kept in the business, and borrowing (Coastline Bank’s loans, the line of credit, the brewer’s instalment plan and, if you count them, the cafés’ leases). At the end of 2027 its interest-bearing debt was $65,250 against equity of $62,818, a debt-to-equity ratio of 1.04. In module 3 she assumed a long-run debt share of 20% of Lantern’s value to work out a cost of capital. Where should a target like that come from? Is debt cheap money, as it looks, or does borrowing only move risk around?

scenes.head: A firm’s capital structure is the mix of debt and equity it uses to finance its assets.

segs.say: A firm’s capital structure is the mix of debt and equity it uses to finance its assets. The question of this lesson is whether that mix changes how much the business is worth. The assets, the coffee, the cafés and the customers, produce the cash. Debt and equity are two ways of dividing that cash among the people who provided the money. Finance theory’s first answer is that the division should not matter; its later answers say why, in practice, it does.

chapters.title: Debt and equity are different claims

scenes.head: Debt and equity are different claims

segs.say: Debt and equity compared

scenes.head: Because lenders are paid first, debt is safer than equity and its required return is lower: in module 3 a lender would charge Lantern 7.5% while its…

segs.say: Because lenders are paid first, debt is safer than equity and its required return is lower: in module 3 a lender would charge Lantern 7.5% while its owners need about 12.8%. That makes debt look cheap. The central lesson of capital-structure theory is that the look is misleading: every dollar of debt makes the remaining equity riskier, and the owners’ required return, the cost of equity, rises to match.

scenes.head: Brookvale Bakeries, a fictional listed chain, has no debt.

segs.say: Brookvale Bakeries, a fictional listed chain, has no debt. Its 100,000 shares trade at $20, so the firm is worth $2,000,000. Its earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) depend on the economy: $120,000 in a recession, $240,000 in a normal year, $360,000 in a boom, each equally likely, and the same pattern is expected for ever, so expected EBIT is $240,000 a year. Ignore taxes for now. The board is considering a recapitalisation: borrow $800,000 at 8% for good and use it to buy back 40,000 shares at $20. The assets and the EBIT are unchanged; only the financing differs.
Brookvale Bakeries (fictional): two capital structures, no taxes

scenes.head: In a normal year leverage raises earnings per share (EPS) from $2.40 to $2.93 and the return on equity from 12.0% to 14.7%.

segs.say: In a normal year leverage raises earnings per share (EPS) from $2.40 to $2.93 and the return on equity from 12.0% to 14.7%. In a recession it lowers them, to $0.93 and 4.7%. The range of EPS between recession and boom widens from $2.40 to $4.00. The two plans give the same EPS when EBIT is $160,000: the level at which the assets earn 8% on their $2,000,000 value, exactly the interest rate. Above it, borrowed money earns more than it costs and the shareholders keep the difference; below it they make up the shortfall. This is the leverage F03 measured with ratios, seen from the shareholders’ side.

scenes.head: Higher expected EPS is not higher value

segs.say: Higher expected EPS is not higher value. Leverage raised Brookvale’s expected EPS and also its risk. Whether the shares are worth more depends on whether the extra expected return is more than enough to pay for the extra risk. Modigliani and Miller showed that, in a market without taxes or other frictions, it is exactly enough and no more.

scenes.head: Franco Modigliani and Merton Miller, who both later received the Nobel prize in economics, asked (in what are now called the Modigliani–Miller…

segs.say: Franco Modigliani and Merton Miller, who both later received the Nobel prize in economics, asked (in what are now called the Modigliani–Miller propositions) what capital structure does to value in a perfect capital market: no taxes, no costs of bankruptcy or of issuing securities, investors and firms borrowing at the same rate, everyone with the same information, and the firm’s investment decisions fixed. Their answer comes in two propositions.

scenes.head: Proposition I.

segs.say: Proposition I. The value of a firm does not depend on its capital structure: V_L = V_U, where V_L is the value of the firm with debt (levered) and V_U its value without (unlevered). The value comes from the assets’ cash flows and their risk; dividing the cash flows between lenders and shareholders does not change their total.

scenes.head: The argument is that investors can borrow on their own account, which is called homemade leverage.

segs.say: The argument is that investors can borrow on their own account, which is called homemade leverage. Suppose levered Brookvale’s equity is fairly priced at $1,200,000. An investor with $12,000 can buy 1% of it (600 shares) and receive 1% of EBIT minus the interest, or she can buy 1% of the unlevered Brookvale (1,000 shares, $20,000) with her $12,000 and $8,000 borrowed at 8%:
Homemade leverage: two ways to hold 1% of a levered Brookvale (fictional)

scenes.head: The payoffs are identical in every state of the economy, so the two positions must cost the same.

segs.say: The payoffs are identical in every state of the economy, so the two positions must cost the same. If levered shares sold for more, investors would make their own leverage with unlevered shares instead and nobody would pay the premium; if they sold for less, investors would buy them and “unlever” by lending. Any capital structure a firm can choose, an investor can copy or undo at no cost, so a firm cannot create value by choosing one.

scenes.head: Proposition II.

segs.say: Proposition II. The cost of equity rises with leverage. Let r_U be the return investors require on the assets (the cost of capital of the unlevered firm), r_D the cost of debt and D/E the debt-to-equity ratio at market values. Then r_E = r_U + (r_U − r_D) D/E. For Brookvale, r_U = 240,000 ÷ 2,000,000 = 12%, and after the recapitalisation D/E = 800,000 ÷ 1,200,000 = 0.667, so r_E = 12% + (12% − 8%) × 0.667 = 14.67%, the expected return on equity in the table. The weighted average cost of capital (WACC) is unchanged: 0.6 × 14.67% + 0.4 × 8% = 12%. Cheap debt is offset, exactly, by dearer equity.
Proposition II without taxes: the cost of equity rises in a straight line with D/E, the cost of debt stays put (while debt is safe), and the WACC stays at r_U.

scenes.head: Proposition II is why “debt is cheaper” is not an argument for borrowing.

segs.say: Proposition II is why “debt is cheaper” is not an argument for borrowing. The owners of levered Brookvale are not wrong to want 14.67% rather than 12%: their shares now carry all of the assets’ risk on a smaller base of equity. Module 3’s relevered beta says the same thing in CAPM’s language.

scenes.head: Why a theory that “doesn’t hold” matters

segs.say: Why a theory that “doesn’t hold” matters. No real market is perfect, so no one believes Proposition I literally. Its value is as a checklist: if capital structure does change value, it must be through something the propositions assume away, such as taxes, the costs of financial distress, information that managers have and investors don’t, or the incentives debt creates. The rest of the lesson takes those in turn.

chapters.title: Adding corporate tax: the interest tax shield

scenes.head: Interest is deductible from taxable profit; dividends are not.

segs.say: Interest is deductible from taxable profit; dividends are not. Every dollar of interest therefore saves the firm T dollars of tax, where T is the corporate tax rate. The saving is the interest tax shield, T × r_D × D a year. If the debt is permanent and as risky as the interest payments, the shields are a perpetuity discounted at r_D, and their present value is T r_D D ÷ r_D = T × D. Proposition I becomes V_L = V_U + T × D. (OpenStax states the annual shield, tax rate × interest; the perpetuity step that turns it into T × D is the standard textbook derivation shown here.)

scenes.head: Put the 25% tax back into Brookvale.

segs.say: Put the 25% tax back into Brookvale. The unlevered firm now earns 240,000 × 0.75 = 180,000 after tax in a normal year and is worth 180,000 ÷ 0.12 = 1,500,000, or $15.00 a share; the government’s claim of $60,000 a year has taken a quarter of the value. Suppose Brookvale borrows $400,000 for good at 8% and buys back shares. Its interest of $32,000 saves 0.25 × 32,000 = 8,000 of tax a year, worth 8,000 ÷ 0.08 = 100,000. The firm is worth 1,500,000 + 100,000 = 1,600,000.

scenes.head: The gain goes to the shareholders when the plan is announced: the share price rises to 1,600,000 ÷ 100,000 = $16.00, so the $400,000 buys back…

segs.say: The gain goes to the shareholders when the plan is announced: the share price rises to 1,600,000 ÷ 100,000 = $16.00, so the $400,000 buys back 400,000 ÷ 16 = 25,000 shares, and the remaining 75,000 shares are worth $1,200,000. Nothing about the bakeries changed. The government’s claim fell, from $60,000 to $52,000 a year of tax, and the shareholders gained the difference’s present value.

scenes.head: With tax, Proposition II becomes r_E = r_U + (r_U − r_D)(1 − T) D/E.

segs.say: With tax, Proposition II becomes r_E = r_U + (r_U − r_D)(1 − T) D/E. For Brookvale, D/E = 400,000 ÷ 1,200,000 = 0.333 and r_E = 12% + 4% × 0.75 × 0.333 = 13%; the shareholders’ $156,000 a year on $1,200,000 confirms it. The WACC, 0.75 × 13% + 0.25 × 8% × 0.75 = 11.25%, is now below 12%, and it keeps falling as debt rises. Taken alone, the tax shield says a firm should borrow almost everything.

scenes.head: Three cautions keep the shield in proportion.

segs.say: Three cautions keep the shield in proportion. It is worth T × D only if the debt is permanent and the firm always has taxable profit to deduct the interest from; a firm with losses, or whose interest exceeds its EBIT, saves nothing on the extra interest. Many tax systems now cap the interest a company may deduct, so check the current rules before counting on it. And investors pay personal tax too: in many systems interest income is taxed more heavily than share returns, which shrinks the advantage, though in a survey of US finance directors only 4.5% said investors’ taxes were important to their debt decisions (Graham & Harvey, 2002).

scenes.head: Financial distress is the condition of a firm that has trouble meeting its obligations to lenders.

segs.say: Financial distress is the condition of a firm that has trouble meeting its obligations to lenders. Its costs fall into two groups. Direct costs are the fees of a bankruptcy or a restructuring: lawyers, accountants, consultants, appraisers, auctioneers. Indirect costs are usually larger and start well before any bankruptcy: customers stop buying a product they fear will not be supported, suppliers demand cash on delivery, good staff leave, managers spend their time negotiating with banks instead of running the business, and assets are sold quickly at low prices.

scenes.head: Distress also changes owners’ incentives, as F00’s lesson on governance and agency showed.

segs.say: Distress also changes owners’ incentives, as F00’s lesson on governance and agency showed. With the firm near default, shareholders gain from risky gambles (risk shifting), because the lenders bear most of a failure. They also lose interest in safe, valuable projects that would mainly rescue the lenders: if a new investment’s payoff would go largely to repaying existing debt, the shareholders who must fund it may turn it down. This is debt overhang, an underinvestment cost of debt. Lenders anticipate all of this and charge for it in advance, so the firm, and therefore its shareholders, bear the expected costs of distress through a higher cost of debt.

scenes.head: The trade-off theory puts the two forces together.

segs.say: The trade-off theory puts the two forces together. Each extra dollar of debt adds tax shield; it also adds to the expected costs of distress, slowly at low debt and quickly as default becomes likely. The value of the firm is
V_L = V_U + PV(tax shields) − PV(costs of financial distress)

scenes.head: and the best capital structure is the debt level at which one more dollar adds as much expected distress cost as tax saving.

segs.say: and the best capital structure is the debt level at which one more dollar adds as much expected distress cost as tax saving. The table uses a stylised assumption for Brookvale with tax: the present value of distress costs is 0.5 × D² ÷ V_U, small for a little debt and rising steeply. The widget below lets you change it.
Brookvale Bakeries (fictional): value against debt under a stylised trade-off, unlevered value $1,500,000, tax 25%

scenes.head: The trade-off theory predicts a target debt ratio for each firm, and predicts which firms should borrow more: those with steady, taxable profits and…

segs.say: The trade-off theory predicts a target debt ratio for each firm, and predicts which firms should borrow more: those with steady, taxable profits and tangible assets that keep their value in distress (property, vehicles, utilities’ networks) can borrow more; those whose value lies in growth opportunities, brands, research or people, which melt away in distress, should borrow less. Ana’s assumed 20% for Lantern in module 3, a target capital structure, is a judgement of this kind. The theory leaves puzzles too. Myers (1984) judged that it explains observed debt ratios only weakly (in his words, with “an unacceptably low R²”), since debt ratios vary widely among apparently similar firms. It also cannot explain why a very profitable firm, with the most taxable profit to shield, would choose little debt, which is what the pecking order below predicts.

scenes.head: The pecking order theory starts from asymmetric information: managers know more about their firm’s prospects than outside investors do.

segs.say: The pecking order theory starts from asymmetric information: managers know more about their firm’s prospects than outside investors do. Investors know that managers acting for existing shareholders prefer to sell new shares when the shares are overpriced, so they read an equity issue as bad news and mark the price down; Myers (1984) notes that, on average, a firm’s share price falls when it announces a share issue. Debt is less exposed to this, because its value depends less on what managers know. Myers (1984), drawing on his work with Nicholas Majluf, set out the resulting order of finance:

scenes.head: Myers (1984), drawing on his work with Nicholas Majluf, set out the resulting order of finance:

segs.say: Use internal funds first: retained profit and cash in hand. Dividends are set with investment needs in mind but are sticky, so internal funds rise and fall with profits.
If outside money is needed, issue the safest security first: debt.
Then hybrid securities such as convertible bonds.
New shares only as a last resort.

scenes.head: In this view there is no target debt ratio.

segs.say: In this view there is no target debt ratio. A firm’s leverage is the accumulated record of its need for outside money: a very profitable firm with few investment needs ends up with little debt, which is the pattern the trade-off theory struggles to explain. Myers reported that, for US non-financial companies over 1973–1982, internally generated cash covered on average 62% of capital spending, and net new share issues were never more than 6% of external financing.

scenes.head: Lantern’s first two years follow the order, for a small-firm reason as well as an information one: Ana kept most of her profit in the business…

segs.say: Lantern’s first two years follow the order, for a small-firm reason as well as an information one: Ana kept most of her profit in the business, borrowed from her bank and a supplier, and sold no shares to anyone else, which would have meant sharing ownership and control. Many owner-managed firms finance the same way.

chapters.title: Agency costs: debt as discipline and as temptation

scenes.head: F00 described two agency relationships and their agency costs.

segs.say: F00 described two agency relationships and their agency costs. Between managers and shareholders, the danger is that managers with spare cash spend it on growth for its own sake or on comforts; debt helps, because interest and repayments must be paid, leaving less spare cash and bringing in lenders who watch. Between shareholders and lenders, debt creates the risk shifting and underinvestment described above, and the temptation to pay out cash to shareholders before the lenders are paid. Debt therefore reduces one set of agency costs and creates another, and a firm’s best capital structure balances these as well as taxes and distress.

scenes.head: Lenders protect themselves with covenants.

segs.say: Lenders protect themselves with covenants. Affirmative covenants require things: audited accounts each year, insurance, upkeep of the assets. Negative covenants forbid things without the lender’s consent: more borrowing, selling major assets, paying dividends above a limit, merging. Financial covenants set ratios: a minimum interest coverage or current ratio, a maximum debt to EBITDA. A maintenance covenant must hold at every test date; an incurrence covenant is tested only when the firm takes an action, such as new borrowing. Breaking a covenant is a default that lets the lender demand repayment, so in practice it starts a renegotiation. Covenants make debt cheaper, because they limit the behaviour lenders would otherwise charge for, at the cost of the firm’s flexibility.

chapters.title: What finance directors say they do

scenes.head: Graham and Harvey surveyed 392 chief financial officers of US companies and published the results in 2002.

segs.say: Graham and Harvey surveyed 392 chief financial officers of US companies and published the results in 2002. On debt policy, almost 60% cited financial flexibility (keeping room to borrow when opportunities arise) and the firm’s credit rating as important or very important; their main aim was preserving flexibility rather than minimising their weighted average cost of capital. About 45% rated the tax advantage of interest as important or very important, but only 21.4% said the same of the costs of bankruptcy or distress. Of the firms, 44% had a strict or somewhat strict target debt ratio or range, 37% a flexible target and 19% none. On the pecking order the evidence was mixed: 46.8% said insufficient internal funds was an important reason to issue debt. Of CFOs who had seriously considered issuing shares, 69% named dilution of earnings per share as important, and about two-thirds said they were reluctant to issue shares they thought undervalued.

scenes.head: Read together, the theories are partial models rather than rivals with one winner.

segs.say: Read together, the theories are partial models rather than rivals with one winner. Taxes push towards debt; distress costs and lost flexibility push back; information problems make outside equity expensive; and agency costs cut both ways. Which force dominates depends on the firm: its taxes, the safety and tangibility of its assets, how much its managers know that investors don’t, and how much spare cash it generates.

scenes.head: Earnings per share with debt

segs.say: Earnings per share with debt: EPS = ((EBIT − r_D D)(1 − T))/N.
EBIT: Earnings before interest and taxes ($).
r_D D: Interest: the rate on debt times the debt ($).
T: Corporate tax rate.
N: Shares outstanding (shares).
With no debt, EPS = EBIT(1 − T) ÷ N.

scenes.head: EBIT at which two financing plans give the same EPS

segs.say: EBIT at which two financing plans give the same EPS: ((EBIT^* − I₁)(1 − T))/N₁ = ((EBIT^* − I₂)(1 − T))/N₂.
EBIT^*: The break-even (indifference) EBIT ($).
I₁, I₂: Interest under each plan ($).
N₁, N₂: Shares outstanding under each plan (shares).
T: Corporate tax rate (it cancels).
It assumes this: The same EBIT under both plans.
For an all-equity plan against a levered one: EBIT* = I × N₁ ÷ (N₁ − N₂). Brookvale: 64,000 × 100,000 ÷ 40,000 = 160,000.

scenes.head: Modigliani–Miller Proposition I

segs.say: Modigliani–Miller Proposition I: V_L = V_U (no taxes), V_L = V_U + T D (corporate tax, permanent debt).
V_L: Value of the levered firm: debt plus equity ($).
V_U: Value of the same firm with no debt ($).
T: Corporate tax rate.
D: Permanent debt, at market value ($).
It assumes this: Perfect capital markets apart from corporate tax; the firm always pays tax; the debt is permanent and its tax shields as risky as the debt.

scenes.head: Modigliani–Miller Proposition II: the cost of equity

segs.say: Modigliani–Miller Proposition II: the cost of equity: r_E = r_U + (r_U − r_D)(1 − T)D/E.
r_E: Cost of equity of the levered firm (%).
r_U: Cost of capital of the unlevered firm (the assets’ required return) (%).
r_D: Cost of debt (%).
T: Corporate tax rate; set T = 0 for the case without taxes.
D/E: Debt to equity at market values.
Without taxes the WACC stays at r_U; with tax it falls as D/E rises. Module 3’s relevered beta is the same relationship in CAPM terms.

scenes.head: Interest tax shield and its present value

segs.say: Interest tax shield and its present value: Tax shield = T × r_D × D a year, PV = (T r_D D)/(r_D) = T D.
T: Corporate tax rate.
r_D: Interest rate on the debt, also the discount rate for the shields (%).
D: Permanent debt ($).
It assumes this: Permanent debt and taxable profit every year. For debt repaid over time, discount each year’s shield separately.

scenes.head: The trade-off theory

segs.say: The trade-off theory: V_L = V_U + PV(tax shields) − PV(costs of financial distress).
V_U: Value of the firm with no debt ($).
PV(tax shields): Present value of the tax saved by deducting interest ($).
PV(costs of financial distress): Present value of expected direct and indirect costs of distress, which grow with debt ($).
The optimal debt level is where the last dollar of debt adds as much expected distress cost as tax saving.

chapters.title: Example: Brookvale’s EPS under two plans

scenes.head: Brookvale’s EPS under two plans

segs.say: Brookvale Bakeries (fictional) has 100,000 shares at $20 and no debt. EBIT will be $120,000, $240,000 or $360,000. The alternative plan borrows $800,000 at 8% and buys back 40,000 shares. Ignore taxes. Find EPS in each state under both plans, and the EBIT at which the plans give the same EPS.

scenes.head: Brookvale’s EPS under two plans

segs.say: Step 4. Check: at $160,000 both plans give EPS of $1.60, and the assets earn 160,000 ÷ 2,000,000 = 8%, the interest rate.

scenes.head: Brookvale’s EPS under two plans

segs.say: All equity: $1.20 / $2.40 / $3.60. Levered: $0.93 / $2.93 / $4.93. The plans tie at EBIT of $160,000.

Borrowing raises EPS whenever the assets earn more than the 8% the debt costs, which they do in a normal year and a boom. It also widens the swing of EPS, so the comparison of expected EPS alone says nothing about which plan shareholders should prefer.

scenes.head: Brookvale’s recapitalisation with tax

segs.say: Now Brookvale pays corporate tax at 25%. Its normal-year EBIT of $240,000 is expected for ever, investors require 12% on the unlevered firm, and it can borrow permanently at 8%. It announces that it will borrow $400,000 and use it to buy back shares. Under Modigliani and Miller with corporate tax, find the firm’s value, the share price after the announcement, the shares bought back, the cost of equity and the WACC.

scenes.head: Brookvale’s recapitalisation with tax

segs.say: Step 3. The announcement moves the value to the shares at once: price 1,600,000 ÷ 100,000 = $16.00. The buyback at that price retires 400,000 ÷ 16 = 25,000 shares, leaving 75,000 worth 75,000 × 16 = 1,200,000, which is V_L − D.

scenes.head: Brookvale’s recapitalisation with tax

segs.say: V_L = $1,600,000; share price $16.00; 25,000 shares bought back; r_E = 13%; WACC = 11.25%.

The shareholders gain $1 a share, all of it tax the government no longer collects. Discounting the unlevered after-tax cash flow at the lower WACC gives the same levered value, which is why a WACC with after-tax debt cost already includes the tax shield. Before taking the $100,000 at face value, ask whether the debt is really permanent and whether Brookvale will always have profit to deduct the interest from.

chapters.title: Example: How much more can Winterbourne Ferries borrow?

scenes.head: How much more can Winterbourne Ferries borrow?

segs.say: Winterbourne Ferries, a fictional listed operator, pays tax at 25% and has $20 million of debt at 6%. Its EBIT is $9 million in a normal year but fell to $4.5 million in its last bad year, after a fuel-price spike. A shareholder group urges it to borrow another $20 million, at 7%, and buy back shares, citing the tax saving. Its loan agreement has a maintenance covenant: EBIT must be at least 3.0 times interest. Assess the proposal.

scenes.head: How much more can Winterbourne Ferries borrow?

segs.say: Step 1. The tax argument: permanent extra debt of $20 million adds 0.25 × 20 = 5 million of tax-shield value, if Winterbourne can always use the deduction.

Step 2. Interest after the borrowing: 20 × 0.06 + 20 × 0.07 = 1.2 + 1.4 = 2.6 million. Coverage in a normal year: 9 ÷ 2.6 = 3.46; in a bad year: 4.5 ÷ 2.6 = 1.73, well below the 3.0 covenant. Today’s bad-year coverage is 4.5 ÷ 1.2 = 3.75.

Step 3. Debt the covenant allows in a bad year: interest at most 4.5 ÷ 3.0 = 1.5 million, so extra interest at most $0.3 million, or 0.3 ÷ 0.07 = 4.29 million of new debt, whose tax shield is worth about 0.25 × 4.29 = 1.07 million.

Step 4. Weigh it: a breach in a bad year would hand the lenders the right to demand repayment exactly when refinancing is hardest and fuel costs are squeezing the business, inviting the indirect costs of distress (suppliers’ terms, cancelled bookings, a forced sale of a vessel). Those costs are not in the $5 million.

scenes.head: How much more can Winterbourne Ferries borrow?

segs.say: The full $20 million adds about $5 million of tax-shield value but would breach the coverage covenant in a year like the last bad one (1.73 times against 3.0). About $4.29 million of extra debt keeps bad-year coverage at 3.0, with a tax shield worth about $1.07 million.

This is the trade-off theory in practice: the tax gain is easy to measure, the distress cost is not, and covenants make the downside concrete. A board would also ask whether a buyback is the best use of the borrowing capacity, which preserves the financial flexibility that finance directors say they value most.

scenes.head: EPS with and without debt: Brookvale Bakeries (fictional)

segs.say: Brookvale’s two plans, with shares bought back at $20. Move EBIT across $160,000 and watch the lines cross. Add tax: both EPS lines fall by the same proportion, so the crossing point does not move. Raise the interest rate and the crossing moves right. scenes.head: Modigliani and Miller: Brookvale Bakeries (fictional)

segs.say: Brookvale as Modigliani and Miller see it: the assets’ beta of 0.8 gives r_U = 12% with an 8% risk-free rate and a 5% market risk premium, and debt costs the risk-free rate. With tax set to None, the WACC stays at 12% at every debt share (Proposition I) while the cost of equity climbs (Proposition II). Switch tax to 25%: the WACC falls as debt rises and the Firm value row shows V_L = V_U + TD. At 25% debt you should see the worked example’s 13% and 11.25%. The widget holds V_U at the after-tax $1,500,000 in both settings, so with tax off its firm value is $1,500,000 rather than the lesson’s no-tax $2,000,000. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: The trade-off: tax shields against distress costs

segs.say: The stylised trade-off. Find the debt that maximises value at the defaults ($375,000), then make distress costs more severe (a business whose value would vanish in distress) or less severe (one with saleable, tangible assets) and watch the best debt level move. Set the tax rate to zero: with no tax shield, any debt only adds distress cost. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: “Debt is cheaper than equity, so borrowing more lowers the cost of capital.”

segs.say: “Debt is cheaper than equity, so borrowing more lowers the cost of capital.”. Debt’s required return is lower, but each dollar of debt raises the cost of equity (Proposition II). Without taxes the two effects cancel exactly; with tax the WACC falls only by the value of the tax shield, and distress costs push it back up beyond some point.

scenes.head: “Leverage raised EPS, so it raised the share price.”

segs.say: “Leverage raised EPS, so it raised the share price.”. Brookvale’s expected EPS rose from $2.40 to $2.93 with no change in value: the extra expected earnings are payment for extra risk. A plan that raises EPS can lower the share price, and one that lowers EPS can raise it.

scenes.head: “The tax shield is always worth T × D.”

segs.say: “The tax shield is always worth T × D.”. T × D assumes permanent debt and a firm that can always use the deduction. Debt that is repaid in five years has five years of shields; a firm with losses or with interest above its EBIT gets no shield on the extra interest; interest-deduction caps can limit it further.

scenes.head: “Financial distress means bankruptcy fees.”

segs.say: “Financial distress means bankruptcy fees.”. Legal and advisory fees are the direct costs. The larger costs are indirect and start before any default: lost customers and suppliers’ credit, departing staff, fire sales, and owners who gamble or refuse good projects because the gains would go to the lenders.

scenes.head: “One capital-structure theory is right and the others are wrong.”

segs.say: “One capital-structure theory is right and the others are wrong.”. Each is a model of one force: taxes, distress, information or incentives. Survey evidence supports parts of several: CFOs value flexibility and ratings, many have targets, and many also prefer internal funds and avoid issuing undervalued shares.

scenes.head: A finance director sets a target.

segs.say: A finance director sets a target. The chief financial officer of a fictional listed food company works out how much debt her firm can carry in a bad year with its covenants and a credit rating she wants to keep, rather than how much would minimise the WACC on paper. She sets a range for net debt to EBITDA, holds the bottom of it in good years so that the firm can borrow quickly for an acquisition, and uses buybacks to stop debt falling far below the range. That is the trade-off theory with flexibility added, which is how the CFOs in Graham and Harvey’s survey describe their own policies.

scenes.head: An analyst reads a leveraged recapitalisation.

segs.say: An analyst reads a leveraged recapitalisation. When a fictional retailer announces it will borrow to buy back a fifth of its shares, an analyst separates the effects. Expected EPS will rise mechanically; that is not news. The tax shield adds value if the retailer has steady taxable profit. Against that, the retailer’s value lies in its brand and its leases, which would lose value fast in distress, so the expected distress cost is high. She also asks why managers chose this moment: a buyback can signal that they think the shares are undervalued, the mirror image of the pecking order’s equity issue.

scenes.head: A small private firm.

segs.say: A small private firm. For a business like Lantern, the questions are the same but the answers are shaped by size. A bank lends against tangible assets and steady cash flow, with covenants; outside equity means sharing ownership, control and information with an investor who will price the uncertainty. That is why small firms lean on retained profit, bank debt and leases, and why the cost of capital estimated in module 3 includes a premium for a small private firm. Whatever the size of the firm, a borrowing plan is worth testing in a bad year as well as a normal one.

scenes.head: What to remember

segs.say: Capital structure is the mix of debt and equity. Debt has a fixed, prior claim, tax-deductible interest and covenants; equity has the residual claim and control.
Leverage raises expected EPS and ROE when the assets earn more than the interest rate, and widens their swings. Brookvale’s plans tie at EBIT of $160,000.
Modigliani–Miller without taxes: firm value and the WACC do not depend on capital structure (homemade leverage); the cost of equity rises with D/E: r_E = r_U + (r_U − r_D)D/E.
With corporate tax and permanent debt, V_L = V_U + TD and r_E = r_U + (r_U − r_D)(1 − T)D/E; the WACC falls as debt rises. Brookvale: $1,600,000, 13% and 11.25%.
The costs of financial distress, direct and indirect, including risk shifting and debt overhang, offset the tax shield: the trade-off theory gives a target debt level.
The pecking order: with asymmetric information, firms use internal funds, then debt, then equity as a last resort, and have no target ratio.

Debt disciplines managers but creates conflicts with lenders, which covenants control. Almost 60% of surveyed CFOs rated financial flexibility and credit ratings important; few aimed to minimise the WACC.

scenes.head: Work the guided problems, then take the knowledge check.

segs.say: That is the whole lesson. Now work the guided problems, with hints when you need them, then try the questions on your own and take the knowledge check. A score of 80 percent completes the lesson.
